sections.heading: Hello and goodbye
sections.body:
The everyday greeting is *bonjour* (hello, good morning, good day). From early evening on, say *bonsoir* (good evening). With friends, family and children, say *salut* — it means both "hi" and "bye".

In France it is polite to add *madame* or *monsieur* when you greet someone you don't know: *Bonjour, madame.* *Bonsoir, monsieur.* Always say *bonjour* when you walk into a shop, a bakery or a doctor's waiting room — skipping it sounds rude.

To leave:

- *Au revoir.* — Goodbye.
- *À bientôt !* — See you soon!
- *Bonne journée !* — Have a good day! (in the evening: *Bonne soirée !*)
- *Salut !* — Bye! (informal)

sections.heading: Tu or vous?
sections.body:
French has two words for "you":

- *tu* — for one person you know well: a friend, a family member, a child, a classmate.
- *vous* — for one person you don't know well or must be polite to (a shop assistant, an official, an older stranger, your boss), and for **any** group of people.

With adults you don't know, start with *vous*. If they say *On peut se tutoyer* (we can say *tu*), switch.

The question "how are you?" changes with it:

- *Ça va ?* or *Comment ça va ?* — How are you? / How's it going? (informal)
- *Comment allez-vous ?* — How are you? (polite)

Typical answers: *Ça va bien, merci. Et toi ?* (to a friend) — *Très bien, merci. Et vous ?* (polite).

sections.heading: Please, thank you, sorry
sections.body:
- *s'il vous plaît* — please (polite, or to several people); *s'il te plaît* — please (to a friend)
- *merci* — thank you; *merci beaucoup* — thank you very much
- *de rien* — you're welcome
- *pardon* — sorry (if you bump into someone), or excuse me (to get past)
- *excusez-moi* — excuse me (to get someone's attention politely)
- *oui* — yes; *non* — no; *non, merci* — no, thank you

In Québec, people often answer *merci* with *bienvenue* (you're welcome), and you will hear *tu* much more than in France.

sections.heading: Pronunciation: rhythm and stress
sections.body:
French doesn't stress one syllable of each word the way English does. Words are grouped into short **rhythm groups**, the syllables are fairly even, and the **last syllable of the group** is a little longer: bon-**jour**, mer-**ci**, au re-**voir**, *Bonjour, ma-**dame**.*

Two things to notice already:

- Many final consonants are silent: *salut* ends in an "u" sound — the **t** is silent; in *s'il vous plaît* you don't hear the **t** of *plaît* either.
- The French **r** is made at the back of the throat, a little like a soft gargle: *merci*, *bonsoir*, *au revoir*.

vocab: how are you?, how's it going? (informal)
examples: Ça va bien, merci. Et toi ?
Very well, thank you. And you?
Goodbye and have a good day!

exercises.prompt: You walk into a bakery at nine in the morning. What do you say first?
At eight in the evening you meet your neighbour, an older man. You say…
Which "you" do you use with a shop assistant?
Which "you" do you use with your little sister?
Which "you" do you use when you speak to two friends at once?
exercises.explain: *Vous* is also the plural: any group of people, friends included.

exercises.prompt: Your friend asks *Ça va ?* A natural answer is…
How do you say "please" to your boss?
Where does the stress fall in *merci*?
options: Both syllables are stressed equally hard

exercises.prompt: Which greeting is only for friends, family and children?
You bump into someone in the street. You say…

exercises.hint: Very well, thank you. And you? (polite)
I'm fine, thanks. And you? (to a friend)
